h1: SEO for solar companies riding the PM Surya Ghar wave
metaTitle: SEO for Solar Companies: Subsidy-Led Demand
metaDescription: SEO for solar companies in India. We capture PM Surya Ghar subsidy searches, state net-metering rules and solar near me intent, then book surveys.
answer: The searches that convert for a solar installer aren't 'best solar panels'. They're 'PM Surya Ghar subsidy for 3 kW', 'net metering rules in Maharashtra' and 'solar installation near me'. Under the scheme, central assistance runs at ₹30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and caps at ₹78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above.
takeaways: Subsidy queries convert several times harder than generic solar terms, because the person searching them has already decided to buy and is now checking the maths.
**Every state is a different product.** DISCOM rules, net-metering caps and state top-up subsidies differ, so one national page cannot serve a Kerala buyer and a Haryana buyer.
A sizing or payback calculator is the best link magnet in this industry — and the best qualifier, because it captures roof area and monthly bill before a salesperson calls.
Residential and C&I are two different websites pretending to be one. The C&I buyer searches CAPEX, OPEX, RESCO and open access; the homeowner searches subsidy and near me.
Never publish a subsidy figure without a source link and a review date. The slabs and the portal process change, and a stale number becomes a customer complaint.

sections.h2: Subsidy search is the demand curve
body: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024, changed rooftop solar from a considered purchase into a subsidised one. That did something specific to search behaviour: it moved the decisive query from `is solar worth it` to `how much subsidy do I get for 3 kW`.

That second query is where the money is. A person asking it has already accepted the premise. They're doing arithmetic, and whoever answers the arithmetic well gets the site survey. Most installer websites answer it with a paragraph that says "government subsidy available, contact us for details", which is the search-marketing equivalent of a shrug.
Publish the slabs. Publish the process. Link the national portal so people can verify you.

callout.title: Date-stamp anything the government controls
callout.body: Slabs, eligibility, the portal workflow and component rules all get revised. Put an "as of" date at the top of every subsidy page, link the national portal as the source, and give one named person on your team a calendar reminder to re-check it quarterly. An out-of-date subsidy figure isn't a ranking problem — it's a customer who signed on the strength of a number you no longer honour.

sections.h2: The process page that removes the fear
body: The second most searched thing after the subsidy amount is how the subsidy actually reaches the customer, because most people assume a government transfer means a year of chasing. Explaining the sequence plainly is one of the cheapest trust-building pages you'll ever publish, and it ranks for a long tail of process queries nobody else bothers with.

Walk through it in order: registration on the national portal, choosing the DISCOM and entering the consumer number, applying for feasibility approval, selecting a registered vendor, installation, applying for the net meter, DISCOM inspection and meter installation, the commissioning certificate, and then the subsidy landing in the bank account.

Then say what nobody says — where it typically stalls. Feasibility approval and the DISCOM meter visit are the two stages that add weeks, and how long they take varies by DISCOM. Being straight about that loses you no customers and wins you the ones who've been lied to elsewhere.

sections.h2: Every state is a different product
body: This is the structural reason solar SEO works, and the reason a single national page fails. Rooftop solar is regulated at state level by the electricity regulatory commission and delivered through the local DISCOM, and the details that decide a customer's payback differ across them.

So build state pages, and build them only for states you actually install in. Each needs an owner and a review date, because these rules genuinely change and a state page that's eighteen months stale is worse than no state page.
bullets: **Which DISCOM serves the consumer**, and its actual application route. A Pune customer and a Nagpur customer may not be dealing with the same office.
**Net metering, net billing or gross metering** — which the state permits, at what capacity, and how surplus is credited or paid. This changes the payback arithmetic more than panel choice ever will.
**Capacity limits** relative to sanctioned load, and what a customer has to do to raise sanctioned load.

**Any state subsidy on top of the central one.** Several states run their own top-up; amounts and caps move, so state the current figure with a source and a date rather than a number you memorised last year.
**Local electricity tariff slabs**, because payback depends far more on what the customer currently pays per unit than on the hardware.

callout.title: Don't build 28 state pages you can't maintain
callout.body: Twelve states you install in, kept current, will outperform 28 generated from a template with a name swapped — and the template version is the scaled-content pattern Google demotes across the whole domain, not just those URLs. Same logic applies to city pages. Build for the places you can actually send a survey team to tomorrow.

sections.h2: Calculators earn links and qualify leads at the same time
body: Solar is one of the few industries where a genuinely useful tool is easy to build and hard to ignore. A sizing calculator and a payback calculator do three jobs at once: they rank, they attract links from local news and community forums, and they collect the two data points your sales team needs before anyone drives anywhere.
Build them around what a customer already knows. Nobody knows their roof area in square feet; everybody knows their monthly bill.

Sizing rules of thumb are standard enough to publish honestly — roughly 100 square feet of shadow-free roof per kW, and roughly four units per kW per day averaged over a year, varying meaningfully with location, tilt, shading and season. Say the range and say why it varies; the installer who admits December output is lower than May output is the one who doesn't get a complaint in December.

Two technical notes. Render the surrounding page server-side with real text — a calculator that exists only as a JavaScript widget gives Google nothing to rank. And don't gate the result behind a phone number. Show the answer, then offer a free site survey; the people who came for the number are the ones who book.

sections.h2: Residential and C&I are two different websites
body: A homeowner in Jaipur and a plant head in Hosur are not the same buyer, and the vocabulary gap between them is total. Trying to serve both from one Solar Services page produces copy that persuades neither and ranks for a muddle of [search intent](/glossary/search-intent) Google can't resolve.
Split the site cleanly at the top level.

sections.h2: Empanelment, the map pack, and the trust problem
body: Two distribution channels decide whether a residential installer gets found, and neither is your homepage.

The first is vendor registration on the national portal, where customers pick an installer from a list. Being on it is table stakes, and the details you supply there — name, address, phone — need to match your Google Business Profile and every directory listing exactly. Mismatched name-address-phone data is the most common reason a legitimate installer can't rank locally.

The second is the map pack for `solar panel dealer near me` and `solar installation in <area>`. That's won with a properly categorised profile, real installation photos with locations, review volume and review replies, and service-area pages only for areas where you've actually installed. Our [local SEO work](/services/local-seo-services) is mostly this.

Then the harder problem. This industry has a trust deficit — subsidy misinformation, fly-by-night installers, systems abandoned after commissioning. That's an SEO opportunity dressed as a reputational headache. Publish your warranty terms in plain language, separating panel performance warranty from product warranty from inverter warranty from your own workmanship warranty. Publish your AMC scope and price. Publish what happens if generation falls short. Name your service turnaround. Every competitor page in your city is silent on all four, and the customer who's been burned once reads exactly that far down.

sections.h2: Budget, timeline and what we guarantee
body: Our SEO starts at ₹75,000 a month, with smaller sites from ₹40,000, ex-GST. Solar tends to need the higher tier once you're across more than two or three states, because each state page carries regulatory detail that has to be verified rather than written. Full numbers are on [pricing](/pricing).

The honest timeline: subsidy and process long tail moves fast — often inside 60 to 90 days — because the competing pages are thin and frequently out of date. `solar near me` map-pack visibility depends on how neglected your profile is; a clean-up can show in four to eight weeks. Competitive national terms like `best solar company in India` take a year and bring tyre-kickers, so we generally don't chase them.

We freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified enquiries from organic search on day one — for most installers that means booked site surveys, not raw form fills. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position for a specific keyword, because nobody controls Google's index. We take three clients a month, which is why the promise is one we can actually keep.

faqs.q: What is the PM Surya Ghar subsidy for a rooftop solar system?
faqs.a: Central financial assistance under the scheme is ₹30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and ₹18,000 for the third kW, which caps total assistance at ₹78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above. Slabs and eligibility can be revised, so publish the figure with a source link and an as-of date.

faqs.q: Which solar keywords actually convert in India?
faqs.a: Subsidy queries, state and DISCOM process queries, sizing and payback queries, and 'near me' installation queries. Those searchers have already decided to buy and are checking the details. Generic terms like 'best solar panels' bring research traffic that rarely books a survey.

faqs.q: Do I need separate pages for each state?
faqs.a: For states you actually install in, yes — net metering rules, capacity limits, DISCOM process and any state top-up subsidy all differ, and they change the customer's payback. What you shouldn't do is generate 28 state pages from a template. Twelve maintained pages beat 28 stale ones, and templated ones risk the whole domain.

faqs.q: Should a solar calculator ask for a phone number before showing results?
faqs.a: No. Gating the number kills the traffic and the links, and the people who abandon at the form were your best prospects. Show the estimate, then offer a free site survey. You still capture roof area and monthly bill, which is what the sales team needed anyway.

faqs.q: How do I rank for 'solar panel installation near me'?
faqs.a: A correctly categorised Google Business Profile, consistent name-address-phone data across the national portal listing and every directory, genuine installation photos, steady review volume with replies, and service-area pages only for areas you've actually worked in. Fabricated locations get profiles suspended.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take for a solar company?
faqs.a: Subsidy and process long tail often moves within 60 to 90 days because competing pages are thin and out of date. Map-pack visibility can improve in four to eight weeks if the profile has been neglected. Broad national terms take a year and mostly bring research traffic rather than surveys.
